content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.

### Forks the batch takes

Each default can be undone and none reverses a decision of his; none touches a model line. Where the record leaves a choice open, the default follows the team's source or the library's way, which the fork names. Those marked **(consequential)** are the three of section 2.

**For the whole batch**

1. **Six rungs, N, C, F, G, S, T, in the manifest's order; C lands only with N; T lands only with N, C, F and S.** Default: so. The way not taken: PLAN's split by area, with walk's numerals in a rung of their own landing with the library's, which no worker could build on the base's library (section 2, reason 1).
2. **The suites each rung runs, once, after its last change of code** (`fortress-repo`, `tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite"). Default: N edits the library, walk and the checker, so it runs `ant testSystem` and `ant testQuick`; C edits the checker and the code generator, so it runs `ant testQuick` once after its pass (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time", step 4); F edits the code generator, the desugarer and walk's phase order, so it runs both; G edits walk only, so it runs `ant testSystem`; S edits walk, a helper and a desugaring phase, so it runs both; T runs the specification's build only.
3. **The stages.** Default: N, C, F and S each run the count stage and the distance stage once on their final tree, against climb batch 28's gate tables, 0 and 0 (F's and S's folds and N's and C's edits change what the stages read); C also times them by P-148, its `change` and `pass` runs against the base's 122 s measured by the prototype on this base build (the prototype, section 4.2), which it cites and does not take again; N times its own count run as its `change` against the same 122 s, since its float tie rule is checking code; G and T change nothing the stages read and list their files (`STAGE_BLIND`).
4. **Appendix I's natives effect** (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:4673-4674`, "twenty-one of the interpreter's object IntLiteral, three of its object FloatLiteral") is made false by N. Default: no rung edits it; the gather writes the merged tree's count there, as climb batch 28's gather did (its fork 5).
5. **The team's tests that the design changes are respelled at the rung that changes each** (review-queue item 444's default): `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss:16` and `:31` and `tests/sequivTest.fss:58` and `:94` in N; the nine compiled tests that write `IntLiteral` and the three pinned messages in C; `tests/LongStringTests.fss:121` and `:141` in G. Each changed line is a point for his sight.
6. **No rung edits the prelude** (P-37). Its `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` keep their names and their arithmetic until the switch-over deletes it; the compiled tests of this batch write those names only as a coercion's parameter type.
7. **The specification's build joins the gather, not the gate** (T), as climb batch 28's V. Default: so; `ant testSpecData` runs in the gate as landed.
8. **microGPT's quick check stays the commit stage's** (P-30; the manual's "Preparing a batch record"). Default: no rung runs it; N changes how walk evaluates every numeral the model writes, and the gather's 52 demos and the commit stage's check see it on the merged tree.

**Rung N**

9. **N1 (consequential). The numeral types as plain value objects with Fortress fields, in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss` beside `Ratio`.** `trait Numeral extends Number comprises { NaturalNumeral, RadixPointNumeral }` declares the four getters abstract; `value object NaturalNumeral(digits: ZZ32, radix: ZZ32, digitValue: ZZ) extends Numeral`, whose `fractionDigits` is 0; `value object RadixPointNumeral(digits: ZZ32, fractionDigits: ZZ32, radix: ZZ32, digitValue: ZZ) extends Numeral`. No binding: walk builds one by its constructor, found as walk's loader finds the library's exceptions (`interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java:281-286`, `getRootValue`). In `FortressBuiltin`, a native component, an object holds no field under walk (row 926), so they leave it. The way not taken: section 2.
10. **N2. The checker's names switch by library**, as `CHARACTER` does (`compiler/Types.java:78-91`): `INT_LITERAL` and `FLOAT_LITERAL` name the prelude's `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` under the compiler's libraries and `FortressLibrary`'s `NaturalNumeral` and `RadixPointNumeral` under the one library. Default: so. The way not taken: rename the prelude's two traits, an edit of the prelude (P-37).
11. **N3. The getters' names and types:** `digits`, `fractionDigits`, `radix`, `digitValue`, the names the prototype proposed (section 7.1), `ZZ32` for the first three and `ZZ` for the value, which a 20-digit numeral needs; `Numeral` extends `Number`, as `IntLiteral` does today, so the library's `excludes` clauses and P-160's Meet Rule readings stand with the names changed. Default: so. The ways not taken: the Draft's letters `n`, `m`, `r`, `v`, which the specification keeps beside each name; `Numeral` outside `Number`.
12. **N4 (consequential; point 3). `RadixPointNumeral` declares `asFloat`, by one rounding, as `NaturalNumeral` does.** Section 2.
13. **N5. One rounding by a new pair of helpers,** a rational `v / r^m` correctly rounded to a double and to a float, in an existing helper class of the float arithmetic or a new one, bound by P-58's form, called by `RR64`'s and `RR32`'s coercions and by both numeral types' `asFloat`; walk's Java conversions call the same Java methods, so the two paths round alike. The prototype's `roundToDouble` and `roundToFloat` in the code generator are the precedent (its section 1, step 3). Default: so. The way not taken: `QQ`'s `asFloat`, `asFloat(num) / asFloat(den)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:656`), which rounds up to three times.
14. **N6. Walk's choice of a declaration reads a numeral argument as the checker does.** A declaration whose parameter at that position is the numeral's own type, or its default, fits the numeral as it is, and the default ranks as no coercion; the most specific of those that fit as they are wins (P-49); if none fits, the coercion attempt runs, and a tie that only numerals make reads each at its default (`Specification/basic/inference.tex`, "A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie", widened by P-173 to float numerals, which read `RR64`). So `x + 1` runs `ZZ32`'s `+` as today, `u = 0` for `u: NN32` runs `NN32`'s pair, `1.0 s` runs `RR64`'s juxtaposition, and `1/2 = 0.5` runs `QQ`'s pair. Default: so. The way not taken: walk's float numeral an `RR64` at evaluation, way F-c, which his default of item 446 declined.
15. **N7. Where walk converts, and how.** At a chosen declaration's parameter, a typed binding, a field and a declared return type, the checker's places, a numeral converts from its exact value: into the eight number types in walk's Java, by the same conversion as the library's coercion, a numeral out of the type's range refused at the place when it runs, as walk refuses one at a binding today (row 325's walk half); into a numeral type as the numeral object; into a program's type through its coercion from the numeral type, called with the numeral object, its result kept for the site so that a site gives one object (review-queue item 440's default); else refused. Elsewhere, an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number` or an unbounded type parameter, it takes its default, as F-74 gives it for integers today. A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default holding them all, by a hook at the head of `EvaluatorBase.inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction` (`EvaluatorBase.java:72-94`), not at its three reads of a value's type, which are G's. Default: so. The ways not taken: a numeral object at every evaluation, which every `i + 1` would pay; conversion at bindings and fields only, as P-172's text names, which would leave a return of `QQ`, `RR32`, `NN32` or `NN64` unconverted.
16. **N8. The pairs, kept and completed.** Every coercion from a numeral type has its pair both ways: the eight number types each with `NaturalNumeral`, `RR32` gaining its coercion from it (P-76; probe 1), and `QQ`, `RR64` and `RR32` each with `RadixPointNumeral`: 11 coercions, 11 pairs at the number types and 11 at the numeral types, each pair's body converting and comparing as the library's do today (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:418`). Default: so. Under walk a pair's body runs with the numeral object; on the compiled path its fold waits for the switch-over (fork F6).
17. **N9. SEQV of two numeral objects inside a coercion's body compares their reduced values,** `digitValue / radix^fractionDigits`, so `2.5` and `2.50` are strictly equivalent there and `0.1_2` and `0.5` are too (P-168's one exception; review-queue item 445's default); walk's rule for value objects field by field takes the two types as its exception. Default: so.
18. **N10. A numeral object prints as the Draft writes a numeral,** its digits in its radix with the radix point after `digits - fractionDigits` of them and `_r` where the radix is not ten, so `C.8_16` in gives `C.8_16` out (the judgement's appendix); a numeral that took its default prints as its type does, `"" 2.50` giving `2.5`. Default: so.
19. **N11. Walk's glue classes of the two objects stay in the tree, unused,** `interpreter/glue/prim/IntLiteral.java` and `FloatLiteral.java`, as climb batch 28's rung R left its own (its fork R3); walk's value classes `FIntLiteral` and `FFloatLiteral` are N's to keep, rework or replace. Default: so; the removal is the names batch's clean-up.
20. **N12. The tests whose answer the design drops.** `tests/XXXRoundNearTieNumeral.fss` asserts 3 and 3 for `round(2.50000000000000001)` and `round(3.49999999999999999)`, where P-173's tie reading gives 2 and 4 on both paths (row 360, closed): it becomes a plain guard under a name of its topic that asserts 2 and 4, by `tests-writing.md`'s promotion steps. `tests/IntLiteralValue.fss` goes with row 578 and the object. `XXXNumeralFloatRungP` (row 443), `XXXNumeralWithNN32` (row 484) and `XXXRadixTenPointNumeral` (row 361) are promoted where your change makes them pass. `XXXextendIntLiteral` and `XXXextendFloatLiteral` name the new types, still refused. Default: so.

**Rung C**

21. **C1. Where the default applies:** exactly P-173's places that fix no type, an untyped binding, a parameter of `Any`, `Object`, `Number` or an unbounded type parameter, a static argument that numerals alone fix, a dotted receiver, and the branches of an `if` or `case` at an untyped binding, which the prototype did not build and the judgement's repair 4 names. Default: so; the prototype's receiver rule, the default only where it has the member, stays (its decision 2).
22. **C2 (point 1). The written-only rule:** a numeral type written as a variable's, field's or return type, or as a static argument, is refused in a program, "IntLiteral cannot be written in a program" in the prototype's words, renamed for both names; files under `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/` are exempt, since the prelude writes `IntLiteral` as return types and no rung edits it (P-37), and N's library writes the numeral types as parameter types only, which its skeptic checks by grep. The rule reads written types, so `t = x` inside a coercion's body binds `t` at the numeral type (review-queue item 443). Default: so. The way not taken: a check of inferred types too.
23. **C3. The static range refusal** (row 325; item 438): a numeral converted at an integer place outside the type's range is refused, and so is a numeral whose one rounding into `RR64` or `RR32` is an infinity. Default: so; P-173 says "a numeral outside the type's range", not only an integer's.
24. **C4. No step 5 and no chain.** `CoercionOracle.buildCoercion` returns the coercion it checks: a program's type with no coercion from the numeral type refuses a numeral (item 439's default), and a numeral's coercion into its default ranks as any coercion. ## 6. A program's own number type, an interval and bfloat16

**The question.** Today a program may declare `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` on its own type (the Working Draft's reason for numeral types, `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-148`). Under B, with the literal types unwritable and no literal value at run time, what does such a type need?

**Under B, as built:** the type declares coercions from the default types, and a numeral at a place of that type takes its default, then that coercion (`viaDefault`). `LiteralOwnNumberCompiled` asserts it, and passes from step 2:
- `a: CC64 = 3` arrives through `coerce(x: ZZ32)` as "`ZZ32 3`";
- `3000000000` through `coerce(x: ZZ64)`;
- the 20-digit `12345678901234567890` through `coerce(x: ZZ)`, exactly;
- `0.5` through `coerce(x: RR64)`;
- the Working Draft's own example `3.1415926535897932384` (`literals.tex:137`) through `coerce(x: RR64)` as "`RR64 3.141592653589793`": the digits past the double are gone before the program's coercion runs, the loss the Working Draft gives as its reason for numeral types ("converting it immediately to a floating-point number may lose precision", `:136-138`);
- an interval `Iv` and a bfloat16 `BF16` with `coerce(x: RR64)` receive the double nearest the numeral: `0.1` arrives as the double `0.1`, and `1.00390625000000000001` as the double `1.00390625`, `1 + 2^-8`, exactly the bfloat16 midpoint (asserted by `SEQV` against typed `RR64` bindings).

**Today, under A.** Measured three ways:
- The compiled path, on the base (`old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base29 ... compile`, scratch `OwnLitInt`, `OwnLitFloat`): `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` receives "`IntLiteral 12345678901234567890`", exact. A type with `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)` receives the literal, but the prelude's `FloatLiteral` offers only `asRR32` and `asRR64` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:996-999`), so it reads "`FloatLiteral 3.141592653589793`" and, in `UserTyToday`, "`FloatLiteral read as 1.00390625`": on the compiled path today a program's type cannot read a float numeral's exact value either. ## 7. Two designs that give a program's type the exact value, by reading

### 7.1 A hybrid

**The hybrid.** B's default where nothing fixes a type; but a program's own type may still declare `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` or `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)` and receives the exact literal, so that a literal value exists at run time only as the argument of such a coercion. This is Haskell's `fromInteger` and `fromRational` for a user's type beside B's (Swift's) default elsewhere; Swift's `ExpressibleByFloatLiteral` hands a `Double` and loses (the coordinator's framing, from their documentation as I know it, not run here).

**What it keeps of B's gains.**
- No literal value at an untyped place, in a generic, at `SEQV`, or in the library's own number types, whose coercions the fold still makes constants. `Cell(3)` a `Cell[\ZZ32\]`, `x SEQV z` true, row 946 gone.
- `IntLiteral`'s 19 operator bindings stay deleted. Of the 24, the literal's accessors that a program's coercion reads must stay, with P-169's compiled carrier: `IntLiteral`'s `asZZ` (`ToZZ`; the other conversions are Fortress text over it) and, optionally, `asFloat` (`AsFloat`, which can be Fortress text over `asZZ`); `FloatLiteral`'s 3; and an accessor for the exact value, which none of the 24 gives (below). So 4 or 5 bindings and one or two new getters, against 24 under A and 3 (walk's, until its rung) under B.

**The accessors.** The Working Draft's four parameters (`literals.tex:110-129`, `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]`): for a numeral with a radix point, the digit count `n`, the count after the point `m`, the radix `r`, and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v`; for an integer numeral, the radix and the value. As getters, not static parameters:
- the one library: `FloatLiteral` declares `getter digits(): ZZ32`, `getter fractionDigits(): ZZ32`, `getter radix(): ZZ32`, `getter digitValue(): ZZ`, and, derived in Fortress, `numerator(self): ZZ` and `denominator(self): ZZ` reduced (`v / r^m`); `IntLiteral` declares `getter radix(): ZZ32` beside `asZZ`. About 10 lines of api and 10 of component, 4 or 5 of them bindings.
- walk's `FFloatLiteral`: its constructor receives the parts (`interpreter/evaluator/values/FFloatLiteral.java:26`, `intPart`, `numerator`, `denomBase`, `denomPower`) but keeps only the text for radix ten and, for any other radix, the text of the nearest double (`:28-31`). It must keep the four fields, and the text, and answer the getters: about 20 lines, plus a glue class for the four getters, or helpers by P-169's device, about 30 lines.
- the code generator's literal node: `FloatLiteralExpr` holds `text`, `intPart`, `numerator`, `denomBase` and `denomPower` (`astgen/Fortress.ast:748-751`), from which `n`, `m`, `r` and `v` follow (`v = intPart · r^m + numerator` where `denomBase = r`, `denomPower = m`; `n` from the text's digits). `forFloatLiteralExpr` must pass them to the compiled `FFloatLiteral`, which today keeps only the text or a double (`compiler/runtimeValues/FFloatLiteral.java`), at a place where the literal stays one; about 15 lines in `CodeGen` and 25 in the class.

**What the checker and the fold do differently.**
- The checker: `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` stay writable only as the parameter type of a `coerce` declaration, and inside its body; the well-formedness check grows by that exception, about 10 lines. At a typed place whose type declares a coercion from the literal type, that coercion is the conversion, before `viaDefault`; today's `buildCoercion` already tries it first.
- The fold: unchanged for the library's number types; it must not fold a program's coercion, which receives the literal value that `forFloatLiteralExpr` and `forIntLiteralExpr` build in their own-type branches, as today.

**The three tests, by reading.**
- *A round trip,* `C.8_16` in and `"C.8_16"` out through a program's coercion: passes if the coercion reads the text (`asString`, kept) or rebuilds it from `n = 2`, `m = 1`, `r = 16`, `v = 0xC8`: "C8" with the point after `n - m` digits, then `_16`. It fails today on walk, which keeps for radix 16 only the nearest double's text (`FFloatLiteral.java:28-31`), and on the compiled path, which hands the coercion a double. A spelling that the four parameters do not hold, a digit-group separator or a radix word, round-trips only through the text.
- *A decimal type* `Dec(unscaled: ZZ, scale: ZZ32)` receiving `3.14159` as `314159` and `5`: passes from `v` and `m` exactly. From a reduced numerator and denominator alone it passes for `3.14159` (`314159/100000` is reduced) but not for `3.14150`, which reduces to `6283/2000` and loses the written scale.
- *`SEQV` by value across radices,* `0.1_2 SEQV 0.5` true and `0.1 = 0.1_16` false: at top level both numerals sit at `Any` and take `RR64`, so `0.5 SEQV 0.5` is true and `0.1 = 0.0625` is false, under B and the hybrid alike (by reading, from 4.4's `1/2 = 0.5`). Between two literal values, inside a coercion's body, `SEQV` must compare the reduced value, not the stored parts: walk's `FFloatLiteral.seqv` compares the nearest doubles (`FFloatLiteral.java:43-48`, marked "HACK"), so it calls two numerals of one double equivalent; the compiled `equality.sEquiv` has no case for `FFloatLiteral`. Both need a reduced-rational comparison, about 5 lines each.

### 7.2 The Working Draft's way: the four numbers as static parameters, by reading

**The design.** A numeral with a radix point has the type `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:110-129`), and a program's type declares `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\])`, whose body reads `n`, `m`, `r` and `v` as values. Reading B's default still applies where nothing fixes a type, so these types live only in the checker; a coercion instantiated for a numeral is realised as the compiled path realises every generic, a class per instantiation with the static arguments stamped in (F-129: "A size read as a value is a constant that the class loader replaces by the numeral").

**What each part must change.**
- *The checker, the numeral's type.* `Misc.scala:468-473` types every numeral as the one `Types.INT_LITERAL` or `Types.FLOAT_LITERAL`; it would type it as the family's instance with four size arguments from the node's parts (`FloatLiteralExpr`'s `intPart`, `numerator`, `denomBase`, `denomPower`, and the digit count from its text). Every test of the literal type by equivalence, `isLiteralType`, `isNumeral`, `numeralReading`, `getCoercionTargetsFrom` (which keeps only coercing traits without static parameters, `CoercionOracle.scala`) and the prototype's default, becomes a test of membership in the family. The library's own `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)` and `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` keep working only if each instance extends a plain `FloatLiteral` or `IntLiteral`, as the Working Draft's "Every numeral also has type `Numeral[\n,m,r,v\]`" (`:127-129`) suggests. About 100 to 200 lines, not sized closer.
- *The checker, the generic coercion.* The compiled path already converts through a coercion with its own static parameter (row 513: "the compiled run converts"), and the coercion oracle instantiates such arrows. Inferring four `nat` arguments from an argument type that writes them is the ordinary inference of F-67. Not tried here.
- *Sizes beyond 32 bits.* A `nat` is an `NN32` value (`SKILL.md`, "Static parameters"), and the checker checks each size against its kind (P-55); `v` of a 20-digit numeral, or of `3.1415926535897932384`, is far beyond it. The checker needs a size kind of arbitrary precision, or `v` split into digits; the class loader already carries a size as a string (`RTTIsize`'s `size` field, `compiler/runtimeValues/RTTIsize.java`) and computes one without checking its kind (row 675, F-146), so its descriptors would hold, but its stamped constant would not (next).
- *The stamped constant.* A size read as a value compiles to `CONST.Nat.<size>`, which the loader replaces by "the IntLiteral of the instantiated number" (`CodeGen.java`, the comment before the `natMethod` call, `:6354` at the base), typed `descFortressIntLiteral`. So today a size read as a value is an `IntLiteral` value at run time; under B it must become a typed constant, `ZZ` for `v`, `ZZ32` for the others, in the loader's `MethodInstantiater`. Not sized.
- *A static range check,* `where { v < 256 }`: no such `where` form is built. P-151 builds three, all of them `T extends SomeTrait` constraints or type variables; a boolean constraint over sizes is not among them (`revival-changes.md`, "Three `where` forms are built"). It would be a fourth form, checked at each instantiation, not sized. With it, an out-of-range numeral is refused at compile time, which the hybrid cannot do.
- *Walk.* Walk has no static types; a `nat` used as a value is an `Int` (row 486), and walk does not apply a coercion with its own static parameter (row 513). It would instantiate the coercion per numeral at run time from `FFloatLiteral`'s parts, which it does not keep (7.1). Waits on P-12; not sized.

**What it gains over the hybrid.** No literal value at run time even for a program's type: the coercion's body sees four constants. No glue binding and no compiled carrier for the literal's accessors, so all 24 can go once walk's rung lands. A static range check, given the fourth `where` form.

**What it costs beyond the hybrid.** The literal types become generic families in the checker; a size kind beyond 32 bits in the checker; typed size constants in the class loader; a boolean `where` form; and walk's instantiation per numeral after P-12. One specialised class per numeral value used at such a type.

**The three tests, by reading.**
- *Round trip* `C.8_16`: passes; the body rebuilds "C.8" from `n = 2`, `m = 1`, `r = 16`, `v = 200` and appends `_16`. A digit-group separator or a radix word does not survive, since no static parameter holds the text.
- *Decimal* `Dec(314159, 5)` from `3.14159`: passes, `v` and `m`; and `3.14150` keeps its scale 5, which a reduced numerator and denominator lose.
- *`SEQV` across radices*: at top level the numerals take `RR64` by B's default, so `0.1_2 SEQV 0.5` is true and `0.1 = 0.1_16` false, as under the hybrid. Two values of the literal types themselves never meet at run time here; as types, `RadixPointNumeral[\2,1,2,1\]` and `RadixPointNumeral[\2,1,10,5\]` differ, so a `SEQV` between them, were one to arise, would be `false` by P-168's rule that values of different types are never equivalent.

  - at a tie (`numeralTie`): each numeral read at its default, the candidates that the arguments so read fit without coercion, then those where only the numerals' positions fit without it.
- The default ranks as no coercion: `counted` (`Functionals.scala`) and `moreSpecificCandidate` (`useful/STypesUtil.scala`) skip a coercion that `LiteralDefaults` made.
- A typed place whose type declares no coercion from the literal type but one from its default takes the default, then that coercion (`viaDefault` in `CoercionOracle.buildCoercion`). This is what lets a program's own type take a numeral (section 6).
- `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` cannot be written outside the library's own files (`TypeWellFormedChecker.scala`): "IntLiteral cannot be written in a program: a numeral has its own type only while the checker types the program." A file counts as the library's when its path holds `/Library/` or `/LibraryBuiltin/`; a type is written by the program when its span's file is the unit's own.
- Joins (`if`, `case`) are not built: an untyped binding of a join of numerals coerces the whole expression, so its branches still make literal values.
- Lines: the whole tree 11 files +231 −59 after step 2.

### Step 3, the fold

- `compiler/desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java` (the phase before the checker): an expression of numerals alone folds exactly into one numeral, the Working Draft's static expressions (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/constant.tex`, "Static Expressions"; `literals.tex:163-173`): `+`, `-`, multiplication, `/` by a nonzero numeral, `^` by an integer numeral (an integer base takes no negative exponent; exponents beyond 4096 do not fold), and a prefix `-` on a float numeral. A result that IEEE arithmetic could make a negative zero does not fold, so `-0.0` stays `-(0.0)` (`StrictEquivalenceRuleCompiled` asserts `0.0` and `-0.0` are not `SEQV`). A result with a radix point, or a quotient, is a numeral with a radix point: in decimal where the denominator divides a power of ten (`10.0^(-5)` becomes `0.00001`), else with the denominator as its base (`1/3`). The visitor's earlier integer folds (comparisons, `DIV`, `MIN`) stay.
- `compiler/desugarer/CoercionDesugarer.scala`: a coercion of a numeral into `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` or `NN64` within the type's range, into `ZZ`, or into `RR64` or `RR32` becomes the numeral typed at that type (`CoercionDesugarer.foldsTo`). Out of range, the coercion call stays, and raises at run time as today.
- `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java`: `forIntLiteralExpr` and `forFloatLiteralExpr` emit a typed numeral's constant, `FZZ32.make(int)`, `FZZ64.make(long)`, `FNN32`, `FNN64`, `FZZ.make(String)`, `FRR64.make(double)`, `FRR32.make(float)`, the floats by one rounding of the exact rational (`roundToDouble`, `roundToFloat`: a quotient of at least 56 or 28 bits with a sticky bit, rounded by `BigInteger.doubleValue`/`floatValue`, scaled by `Math.scalb`). A numeral still of its own type gets the same one-rounded double (row 862). `QQ` is not folded: the prelude has no `QQ` to test it against, so a numeral at a `QQ` place still calls the coercion with a literal value.

No line of either program needs a change.

## 5. The library's own numerals that the default retypes

From the checker's output, `FORTRESS_LITERAL_TRACE=1 java ... WorldFlip -stop check <component>`, on the `FortressLibrary` component, and on `String` at step 2:

<!-- Judgement of the curator's numeral design of 2026-11-08 (machine defaults where no type is declared; the Working Draft's numeral types as fields; a program's type coerces from the numeral type once at load), for the coordinator, before it goes to POSITIONS and a batch. Read-only: nothing in the tree was changed, built or committed. Sources: the brief, the Working Draft (`Specification-1.0-frozen/`), the record, the three reviews and the prototype of 2026-11-08. -->

# Judgement: the numeral design of 2026-11-08

## 1. Coherence

The design is one rule: a numeral converts where it stands, into the declared type, else into the machine default. Six cases get two answers or none; each has a repair.

- Undefined: what "fixes a type". Point 1 lists `Any`; the fork review adds `Object`, `Number` and an unbounded `T` (§1.1); the prototype defaulted at all (probe §1, step 2). Repair: a place fixes a type when its declared type declares a coercion from the numeral type (the eight number types; a program's type by point 4) or is a numeral type; every other type, and no type, takes the default. Then `f(3)` at `Number` is a `ZZ32`, and a tuple at `Any` defaults element by element.
- Two answers: "by its value" where the value is unknown. Row 946 shows it: a variable of numeral type reads `ZZ32` whatever its value. Inside `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, `t = x` is such an expression; so is a `nat` used as a value, whose value a template does not know (probe §8). Repair: the default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of numeral type; a `nat` used as a value has the type the Draft gives, `NN32` (`trait-parameters.tex:84-86`), or `ZZ32` (P-40), chosen once.
- Two answers: the fold against the fields. Point 4 reads the written numeral's four numbers; point 5 folds `7/2`, `-3` and `0.1 + 0.2` into "one numeral", which has no written form: the prototype made `1/3` a radix-3 numeral (probe §1, step 3), and a negative result has no `nat v`. Repair: the fold yields a constant with a sign, as the Draft's `IntegerConstant[\false, 3+5\]` has one (`constant.tex:49-52`): an integer constant defaults as an integer numeral, a quotient to `QQ`, one with a radix point to `RR64`; a program's coercion sees the four numbers of a written numeral only.
- Two answers: a static argument that several numerals fix. `<|3000000000, 0.5|>` is a `List[\RR64\]` if each numeral converts exactly into one instantiation, refused if each defaults first (`ZZ64` into `RR64` is written, P-74); an `if` join likewise. Repair: the narrowest default holding every value, `RR64` where any has a radix point, each converting into it exactly: the tie rule's form (`inference.tex:313-317`).
- Two answers: a program's type with no coercion from the numeral type. The prototype chained default and own coercion (probe §10, decision 3); the Draft says coercion does not chain (`conversions-coercions.tex:407-408`). Repair: refuse, or name the chain as the one exception.
- Undefined: "once per class, at load" as a semantics. For a reference object two evaluations of `c: CC64 = 3` become one object, which `SEQV` sees (`objects.tex:51-53`), and a raising coercion fails at load. Repair: a numeral at a program's type denotes one object, as a string literal does (P-171), or hoist value types only.
- One answer, for the record: `-3` is `-` on a numeral (`lexical-structure.tex:1053-1080`); folded, `-2147483648` fits `ZZ32` and `u: NN32 = -3` is refused. `x = 3` then `x` at `ZZ64` converts (P-74), at `NN32` is refused (fork §6.1), point 1's rule. `pi: RadixPointNumeral` (`Constants.fsi:16-17`) is refused by the fifth default and becomes `RR64`. Two numeral values inside a body: by P-168 value objects compare field by field, so `2.5` and `2.50` differ there, as the Draft's types differ; elsewhere both default and are `SEQV`.

## 2. Against the record

- Revised: P-76 (the name; "walk's half" once walk has static types, which the default makes walk's rule today; `IntLiteral`'s arithmetic, which the fold retires). P-172: the name; "Where nothing fixes a type ... the numeral stays an exact `FloatLiteral`: `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\FloatLiteral\]`"; "prints a bare numeral as written, as the team's `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss:16` asserts", a team test that now breaks; its two open items close.
- Facts: F-79, F-57 (the checker's two types), F-169 (the text's `IntLiteral`), F-73 (the tie reading becomes the rule, floats included), F-74 (walk's numeral by value, a gap made the rule), F-118, F-262. P-169: the 24 numeral glue bindings and their carrier fall away (probe §4.5).
- Bent: P-26. The prelude keeps the numeral's type at every untyped place (fork §3.3), code "built alike for all its types"; the Draft's types are unfinished text (F-169), the names the implementers' later word. No team word calls them temporary (scout §10). The one team word for point 4: "IntLiterals should always be transient objects with minimal lifetime" (`compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:21-23`, 2009). The entry should own the weighing as the curator's.
- Unchanged: P-168, P-171, P-165 (a name only), P-49, P-46, P-40, P-74.

## 3. Against the Draft

- Kept as written: `literals.tex:25-26` (literals are values); `:141-148` (library designers decide by coercions; coercions to integers and rationals); `:163` (`3.125` is `3125/1000`, at a `QQ` place); `:170-173` (one rounding); `variables.tex:75` (the variable's type is the initializer's).
- Changed in form: `:83-129`, the four numbers as fields, `Numeral` the supertype, `Literal[\v\]` and the two `WithExplicitRadix` types folded into the radix field; `constant.tex:44-74`, a folded expression is a numeral, not a constant trait; `conversions-coercions.tex:98-101`, a conversion also where no type is declared, which that list excludes: the default is a rule beside coercion.
- Contradicted: `:132-141`, "not directly converted ... polymorphic ... may lose precision", at places that fix no type: `y = 3.1415926535897932384` then `q: QQ = y` is refused, `r32: RR32 = y` rounds twice (fork §6.1); the restart's `QQ`/`NN` (`literals.tick:25`, context by P-25).
- The binary chapter (`binary.tex:1601-1602`, `:1637-1640`): a coercion from `NaturalNumeral[\m,radix,v\]` `where { radix = 2^q, q DOT m = n DOT 2^bk }`, and `opr ||` into `LinearSequence[\BinaryWord[\b\], n+k\]`. Can give: the coercion into a word of written width, reading `radix` and the digit count at load and raising on a bad radix or width. Cannot give: the width `k` from the digit count as a static size, so `||` with a numeral has no static result type; `where` over the numbers (no built form, P-151).

## 4. The sub-choices

- `=` pairs stay and fold: follows from P-165 with point 1; without them `u = 0` for `u: NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32` falls to `SEQV`, `false` (probe §5, §9). "Fold" means: the pair's conversion of its numeral runs at compile time, as at any typed place.
- `gg(5, w)` takes the `ZZ32` declaration: follows from point 1 with P-49. Flips `InferO2Pos:18-19` and `inference.tex:186`.
- `x = 7/2` a `QQ`, a comparison of literals folds: conflicts with point 5 as prototyped (`7/2` → `RR64`, decision 4); coherent with repair 3, after which `1/2 = 0.5` is `true` through the kept pair and the comparison need not fold. The Draft (`:163-166`, a rational static expression), the restart and the library's `/` favour `QQ`.
- A numeral type written only as a coercion's or operator's parameter type: follows from point 4; must also cover inferred types (repair 2). Breaks 9 team and 10 revival tests that write `IntLiteral` (probe §4.3): a point to report.
- An expression of numerals folds exactly: free. The alternative, numeral types with no arithmetic, makes `3 + 4` `ZZ32` arithmetic and `2147483647 + 1` an overflow. The Draft (`:165-173`) and P-171's string fold favour the fold; it needs repair 3 and the prototype's exceptions (`-0.0`, `1/0`; decision 5).
- Strings: P-171, decided; independent of points 1 to 4.

## 5. The test cases

The appendix lists 42 programs with the design's answer, today's, and a mark: [P] the prototype measured it, [W] a review on walk, [R] by reading. Those that separate it from today: `x SEQV z` and `Cell(3)`, where the paths first agree; `"" 2.50` and `NumberPrintTest:16`, printing the double; `q: QQ = y` refused for `y = 0.1`; `g(bigN)` (row 946 closes); `z: ZZ32 = 3000000000`, static where the prototype left it at run time; the own-type cases; `C.8_16` round-tripped, which no path gives; microGPT, no line and no bit changed, by reading only (probe §4.7).

## 6. Open for the curator

- Out-of-range at a typed place: static (point 2) or run-time (the prototype).
- A program's type with no coercion from the numeral type: refused, or default then coerce.
- "Once per class": one object per site as a rule, or value types only.
- A `nat` used as a value: `NN32` (the Draft) or `ZZ32` (P-40).
- The fold's result: a signed constant with three defaults, or the Draft's constant traits.
- A numeral-typed value inside a coercion's body: bindable by inference, or only the parameter.
- `NumberPrintTest:16` and the 9 team tests writing `IntLiteral`: respelled, or kept red.
- `SEQV` of two numeral values: by fields (P-168) or by reduced value (probe §7.1).
- Walk before P-12: the float numeral defaults at evaluation (F-c) or converts place by place.
- The binary chapter's `||` with a numeral, and `constant.tex:84-87`'s numeral `||`: dropped, folded, or given a written size.

## Summary

Verdict: coherent with the changes named below; as stated, four cases get two answers and two are undefined.

The design's one rule, convert where the numeral stands, into the declared type or else the machine default, answers the ordinary cases alike on both paths. The changes it needs: define "fixes a type" as a declared type with a coercion from the numeral type; apply the default to numerals only, never to an expression of numeral type, and give a `nat` used as a value one type; let the fold yield a signed constant whose quotient defaults to `QQ`, so that `x = 7/2` stays a `QQ` and `-2147483648` fits `ZZ32`; instantiate a type parameter that several numerals fix at the narrowest default holding them all; say whether a program's type without a coercion from the numeral type is refused or chained; and state "once per class" as a rule about objects, or hoist value types only.

It revises P-76 and P-172 (the names, the exact-where-unfixed clause, printing as written), six facts, and bends P-26, which the entry should own as the curator's weighing: the team's one word for it is that literals "should always be transient objects". Against the Draft it keeps literals as values, coercions as the library's device and one rounding; makes the four numbers fields; and contradicts "not directly converted" at untyped places and the binary chapter's static width, which fields cannot feed.

The sub-choices follow from the points, except `x = 7/2`, which needs the fold repaired, and the fold itself, which is free and which the Draft favours. Forty-two programs pin the design; the prototype measured most compiled ones; microGPT changes no line and no bit, by reading only. Ten questions stay open.

#!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}

(* ZZ32's CHOOSE gives the exact binomial coefficient, throws IntegerOverflow exactly where the coefficient does not fit, and keeps its values in a parallel loop. *)
component ChooseZZ32Walk
export Executable

overflows(n: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): Boolean =
  try
    ignore(n CHOOSE k)
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => true
  end

pair(n: ZZ32): ZZ32 = if n MOD 2 = 0 then (n DIV 2) (n - 1) else n ((n - 1) DIV 2) end

All literals represent value objects; therefore their values do not have object identity.

=== Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:110-148
A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point) has type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
interpreted in radix ten.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
be the radix) has the following type:
\begin{Fortress}
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
\end{Fortress}
where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.

Every numeral also has type
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.


Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect them to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it immediately to a floating-point number
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used in an expression
involving floating-point intervals,
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).

=== Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/constant.tex:44-90
\item The \emph{constant} traits, which describe values denoted by
expressions composed from literals and operators (described in
\secref{constant-values});
the type of a constant expression encodes the value of the expression.
For example, the type of a constant expression \EXP{3+5},
%IntegerConstant[\false, 3+5\]
\EXP{\TYP{IntegerConstant}\llbracket\VAR{false}, 3+5\rrbracket},
encodes the value of the expression; the operator \EXP{+} is
used in the static arguments.  When an operator is not supported in static
arguments, \library\ can still encode the value of the expression by
providing a specific constant trait such as
\EXP{\TYP{RationalValueTimesPi}\llbracket\VAR{false},1,1\rrbracket}
(described in \secref{pi}).



\item The \emph{static} traits, which describe values denoted by
expressions composed from literals, operators (described in
\secref{constant-values}), and \KWD{bool}, \KWD{nat},
and \KWD{int} parameters; here the type
does not encode the value of the expression, but the value of the
expression can nevertheless be known statically if specific
values are specified for the static parameters.  Also, in situations
where the type of an expression composed solely from literals and
operators nevertheless cannot be described by a constant trait, then a
static trait may be used to describe it instead.
For example, a static expression \EXP{2(3+m)} where \VAR{m} is a
\KWD{nat} parameter has trait \TYP{NaturalStatic}.
\end{enumerate}


The only operation on literals that produces a new literal (as opposed
to a constant) is concatenation by using the operator \EXP{\|}.
One may concatenate mixed string and
character literals, producing a string literal.
For example, ``\txt{foo}''\EXP{\|}''\txt{bar}'' yields ``\txt{foobar}''.
One may also concatenate two natural numerals
of the same radix, producing a new natural numeral of that radix.
For example, \EXP{\mathtt{deadc}_{16} \| \mathtt{0de}_{16}} yields \EXP{\mathtt{deadc0de}_{16}}.

Every literal trait extends an appropriate constant trait, and every
constant trait extends an appropriate static trait.  So every
literal is also a constant expression, and every constant expression
is a static expression.

=== Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:130-178


Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect them to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it immediately to a floating-point number
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used in an expression
involving floating-point intervals,
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
In \library, every numeral without a radix point has the type
\TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the number types
(\secref{basic-rationals}); each of the five integer types
(\secref{basic-integers}), \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a
coercion from it.
\revision{revival-numeral-type}{The Working Draft of February 2011 described
the numeral types above, which no library declares, and did not name the type
that \library\ give a numeral.
The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that a numeral has a type of its own,
\TYP{IntLiteral}, from which each number type converts, the type the compiled
path's own library gives it, and \library\ now declare it so.
The compiled type checker gives every numeral without a radix point that type.
The interpreter does not yet: it gives such a numeral the type
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value
does not fit in the narrower type, and it is to give it the type
\TYP{IntLiteral} once it runs with the static types of the compiled type
checker.}


\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
number types (\secref{literals}).
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
value does not fit in the narrower type.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values.

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.

- a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, an integer, a character or a boolean by its value, and a float by its bits;
- a reference object, a string among them, is equivalent only to itself;
- a function is equivalent to itself, but may be found unequal to another that behaves the same.

So for a value object `V` without its own `=`, `V(s) = V(t)` is `false` where `s` and `t` are equal strings made by two computations. Two string literals of one text are one object (P-171).
